initial_observation.encounter_context: admitted to the hospital due to a 2-month history of progressive episodes of disorientation, inattention, frequent forgetfulness, confusion, sporadic nocturnal visual hallucinations, and occasional difficulties in naming objects
initial_observation.chief_complaint: progressive episodes of disorientation and cognitive disturbances
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Patient was admitted with symptoms that began coinciding with initiation of immunotherapy with nivolumab and ipilimumab and included asthenia, adynamia, mild gait instability, heat intolerance, nocturnal sweating, palpitations, tremors, low mood, and deterioration in quality of life and functionality.
presenting_symptoms: deterioration in quality of life and functionality
known_prior_history: predominantly epithelioid pleural mesothelioma treated with pemetrexed and cisplatin chemotherapy
locoregional progression at 6th year of follow-up
palliative immunotherapy with Nivolumab and Ipilimumab started

evidence_items.source_text: At evaluation, the patient was partially disoriented, inattentive, with mild ataxia and dysarthria upon neurological examination. Her vital signs and the rest of the physical examination were without relevant findings.
Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed non-confluent supratentorial white matter microangiopathy, without evidence of vascular lesions or mesothelioma dissemination;
lumbar puncture showed no signs of encephalitis or leptomeningeal spread.
Further investigations revealed a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), prompting a comprehensive evaluation of the thyroid axis.

The results demonstrated elevated levels of peripheral thyroid hormones (total T4 and T3), absence of anti-thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies (TRAb) and anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO), along with the presence of anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibodies.
subsequent thyroid iodine uptake studies indicated low uptake.
Ultimately, it was concluded that the etiology of the delirium was a thyrotoxicosis episode that developed in the context of autoimmune thyroiditis, secondary to ICI treatment.

Symptomatic treatment with beta-blockers was initiated, leading to a gradual amelioration of neurological manifestations. Upon discharge, the patient was scheduled for outpatient monitoring by an endocrinologist and advised to continue her oncological regimen without modifications.

accepted_aliases: thyrotoxicosis secondary to immune checkpoint inhibitor induced thyroiditis
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Further investigations revealed a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), prompting a comprehensive evaluation of the thyroid axis. The results demonstrated elevated levels of peripheral thyroid hormones (total T4 and T3), absence of anti-thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies (TRAb) and anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO), along with the presence of anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibodies. No additional endocrine irregularities were detected, and subsequent thyroid iodine uptake studies indicated low uptake. Ultimately, it was concluded that the etiology of the delirium was a thyrotoxicosis episode that developed in the context of autoimmune thyroiditis, secondary to ICI treatment.
